The Damon/Kimmel faux feud has been going on for decades at this point, and it just never gets old. Matt Damon and Jimmy Kimmel have been pretending to hate each other for years, doing bits about it at the Oscars and on Kimmel’s talk show. And despite actually being great friends, they love to keep this bit going. On that note, the talk show host was recently asked to give a toast to Matt Damon at a huge Hollywood event, and there's a hilarious video that I just can't get enough of!

Damon has had quite a year, having released The Rip, which co-stars his best friend, Ben Affleck. The Rip was also a huge hit for Netflix and allowed for him to continue to work with Affleck amid other projects at their production company. Damon was also most notably the star of The Odyssey, which grossed well over a billion dollars worldwide and is an awards season favorite. As a result, GQ named Damon one of their Men of the Year in their annual issue. At the party to celebrate the magazine. Jimmy Kimmel gave quite the speech, which you can see below:

Kimmel, of course, couldn’t resist mentioning some controversial people named in GQ magazine over the years to compare Damon, too. On top of that, the talk show was quick to say that Tom Holland was more deserving of this honor. Kimmel said:

Matt had a big year and he's in great company. I've made a list of some of the other honorees. Mel Gibson, 1996, 2007, Kanye West. The list goes on and on and you you deserve it. You really do. Not as much as others might deserve it. You know, Tom Holland was in the Odyssey and Spider-Man this year. He was in number one and number two. You're just number two. You're a big number two. You deserve this.

Kimmel then toasted to his faux foe and fittingly called him “Mrs. Ben Affleck.” Of course, Damon had his own hilarious quips as a response. He was quick to point out one key detail about that night, saying:

I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place.

Of course, this is all in good fun, and the riffing is expected any time these two guys are in the same room together. It started back in the early 2000s when Jimmy Kimmel started saying “Apologies to Matt Damon, we ran out of time” at the end of every show. It was a self-deprecating joke, as a way to make fun of how terrible his guests were when his show first started, as opposed to having a movie star like Damon. It became a running joke that continued even as Kimmel’s show became more successful.

Periodically, Damon tries to sneak onto Kimmel’s show, and the host jokingly refuses to have the actor on as a guest. They also make fun of each other relentlessly in public, and hilariously compete for the affection of Ben Affleck. It’s a great bit, and if this GQ speech is any indication, this duo isn’t planning on retiring the quips anytime soon. I hope they continue to dig at each other for years to come, because it is just too much fun to watch.

Fans can check out Matt Damon in The Odyssey, which is still playing in select theaters nationwide. It’s the tail end of The Odyssey’s historic box office run, so make sure to see it on the big screen while you still can. You can also watch Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which airs at 11:35 p.m. ET on ABC and is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3651. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

The US president doesn't seem too concerned about the potential risks to US national security: "I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A CNBC report says the return of disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang is not being considered by Nvidia's board of directors, despite a rising chorus of billionaire voices calling for it—including, earlier today, that of US president Donald Trump.

"I would not mind. I would not mind that," Trump told reporters in response to a question about Huang's possible return (via Reuters). "I like—I threw out the name of Tim Cook. But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement—I think he learned a big lesson, I guess. Maybe one lesson's more important than another. But I would certainly not mind seeing that."

Asked about US intelligence reports that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Trump said he doesn't know whether she's a spy, and that "a lot of people" are asking Huang to return to the CEO's role.

"They think Jensen should go back," Trump said. "That certainly isn't a bad idea." He also said that US national security was not put at risk by Huang's deep ties to Trump, adding that "China plays games with us, so we play games with China."

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, shortly after his affairs with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence as well as multiple Nvidia employees came to light. Calls for his return were almost immediate, mostly notably from billionaires like Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, but also Nvidia employees and fans. Tech executives have reportedly launched a "war room" to lobby for his return, and Huang himself is apparently open to the idea.

Whether Nvidia feels the same is another matter: An anonymous source told CNBC that the board is not considering bringing him back, and is instead focusing on an investigation into Huang's affairs and whether he compromised US national security or Nvidia itself.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, one of Trump's most vocal and reliable supporters, also recently seemed to dismiss the idea, saying Nvidia "needed a dramatic shakeup" at the top and that it should look "outside the company" for a new chief executive. It remains to be seen whether any of those positions change in light of Trump's support.

#3648. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

If you'd like to reminisce a bit before the long-awaited game finally hits, you can check out our favourite Grand Theft Auto pieces Eurogamer's published over the years.

Fans are really going to want to try this out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of films left impressions on the 2026 movie schedule, but few managed to really hit the zeitgeist like Project Hail Mary did. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s science-fiction epic – based on Andy Weir’s 2021 book of the same name – managed to capture audiences’ imaginations (and make some solid money at the box office in the process). Anyone who needs further proof of the film’s popularity should know that a mixed-reality game is in the works and, to quote Rocky, the description of his role sounds “amaze.”

This new game – Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars – hails from game studio Maze Theory and takes place during a formerly untapped period of time within the main story. It specifically takes place after Dr. Ryland Grace saves his alien companion, Rocky, and before they return to the latter’s homeworld, Enid. Players take on the role of Dr. Ryland Grace (played by the impeccable and expressive Ryan Gosling in the film) and, as SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend learned from the developers, the game gets quite immersive.

Players can interact with objects, steer the titular ship (Hail Mary), repair it and even complete tasks like opening cupboards. One also only needs a headset to further immerse themselves in the game’s story, which was also talked out with Weir. Of course, all the while, fans can also interact with Rocky (who is not a pet) throughout their travels, and he’ll be actively watching your moves and providing feedback. Gameplay lead Sandy Lockie told SFX this about bringing Rocky and Grace’s relationship to the game:

We wanted to do justice to Rocky and Grace and their relationship. Sometimes they’ll be crabby with each other, sometimes they’ll get a little bit down and need the other one to pick them up.

It just wouldn’t have made sense to craft a game like this without including Rocky in some form or fashion. Since the film’s release he’s become something of a sensation, and he went viral after Amazon posted a video of the character watching himself. Even Neil DeGrasse Tyson praised the character’s design and noted that Weir and the filmmakers avoid the Hollywood trope of making him a humanoid. Judging by Lockie’s comments, even the Maze Theory team was taken with Rocky while they were testing the game:

Even when we’re testing, although you know he’s a character and isn’t really there, I’ll talk to him: ‘Well, what do I do here?’ He has good suggestions and sometimes bad suggestions. It’s one of those things that your brain just kind of lunges into, like, ‘Yep, Rocky’s there. He’s a character now!’ He’ll do jazz hands or prompt you to play rock-paper-scissors and all sorts of stuff . It’s fun to step into that and feel like he’s your friend and companion, your little explorer buddy.

All in all, this game should provide fans with a bit of a taste of being in Ryland’s shoes and present the opportunity to catch up with Rocky in some sense. Project Hail Mary’s ending may have closed the book on Grace and Rocky’s bromance for now, but I still like the idea of people being able to create their own moments reminiscent of the film’s best scenes. So, on that note, why not jump into this sweet-sounding extension of the PHM story?

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is now available Pico, Meta and Android XR. Also, fans can grab a Prime Video subscription and stream the movie on which the game is based right now.

#3645. GTA 6 Hacker Pleads Guilty To Cybercrimes After Infamous 2022 Leak

Arion Kurtaj, the then-17-year-old hacker who allegedly leaked early Grand Theft Auto 6 footage back in 2022 after hacking into developer Rockstarâs servers, has officially pled guilty to the crime four years later.

The BBC reports that the now-21-year-old pled guilty at the Woolwich Crown Court in London today, November 16, both to the Rockstar hack that leaked early in-development footage of GTA 6, and to several other cybercrimes carried out as part of the hacking gang Lapsus$. The entire saga has been wild to watch unfold. Kurtaj first hacked into Rockstar’s servers while on bail for other crimes, and was able to do so with an Amazon Fire Stick in a hotel room while under police protection. He then posted in the companyâs Slack threatening the company if it didnât negotiate with him over Telegram. He pled not guilty in 2022.

Initially, Kurtaj was deemed unfit to stand trial, with medical professionals citing his acute autism as cause to have him instead sentenced to life in a hospital prison. However, in January 2026 it was determined he was now fit to stand trial, and he subsequently pled guilty. His sentencing will be scheduled for a later date.

A Message from Rockstar Games pic.twitter.com/T4Wztu8RW8

— Rockstar Games (@RockstarGames) September 19, 2022

Rockstar refused to negotiate with Kurtaj at the time, but the studio has acknowledged the entire thing over the years, with Grand Theft Auto 6âs second trailer containing what seems to be a joke poking fun at the hack asÂ  the gameâs co-lead Jason says that heâs âfixing some leaksâ while patching up a roof. This would only be the first of several leaks GTA6 would be subject to, as the game was subsequently leaked over the course of several weeks earlier this year by someone going by Cyberleek, who posted multiple clips of what seems to be an early build of the game.

#3644. Original GTA 6 leaker pleads guilty to hacking Rockstar Games, years after first revealing Lucia

The 21-year-old responsible for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking in-development GTA 6 footage in 2022 has pleaded guilty to a number of offenses.

The GTA 6 leaker was initially sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to his severe autism, but was more recently deemed fit for trial and moved to a regular prison earlier this January. On Monday, at the Woolwich Crown Court in South East London, he pleaded guilty to hacking Rockstar Games and a number of other companies, including Uber and EE/BT, in cyber attacks estimated to have caused £10m in damages.

At the time of his Rockstar hack - when he was between the ages of 16 and 17 - the leaker was already under police protection at a Travelodge hotel to keep him from rival hackers he had allegedly stolen Bitcoin from. Somewhat surprisingly, he then managed to hack the multi-billion dollar game maker with nothing but an Amazon Fire Stick, the hotel room's TV and a bluetooth-connected keyboard and mouse.

As the BBC reports, he also managed to break into the developer's Slack channels, before threatening to release the GTA 6 source code if Rockstar failed to contact him within the day. The leaker has yet to be sentenced.

Those 2022 leaks were quite substantial, too, revealing about an hour of unfinished gameplay and clueing the world in on Lucia's existence - the series' first female protagonist in years. Of course, those 2022 leaks shouldn't be confused with 2026's, which saw Cyberleek spill nuggets of nearly finished clips onto the internet, despite Rockstar's best efforts to keep GTA 6 a closely guarded secret.

"We recently suffered a network intrusion in which an unauthorised third-party illegally accessed and downloaded confidential information from our systems, including early development footage for the next Grand Theft Auto," Rockstar said at the time, before it had officially unveiled GTA 6. "At this time we do not anticipate any disruption to our live game services, nor any long-term effect on the development of our ongoing projects. We are extremely disappointed to have any details of our next game shared with you all in this way."

Four years later, GTA 6 is finally around the corner - you're probably already aware considering the marketing frenzy Rockstar's been drumming up.

While it’s been over three decades since the final Full House episode aired, DJ Tanner actress Candace Cameron Bure still feels her TV “family” is important to her. So, you can only imagine how emotional the TV actress’s tribute was for her TV dad, Bob Saget, on the fourth anniversary of his death this year. If you want to get more in your feels, Bure shared her sweet reaction to BTS footage showing her and Saget on set. Fans, prepare to bring out the tissues.

Since Bob Saget died in 2022 due to accidental blunt head trauma, Candace Cameron Bure said it’s been hard watching Full House clips. But after ET showed her throwback clips from 1994 of her and Saget together on the set of the sitcom (as well as an earlier joint interview with John Stamos), it brought out all kinds of emotional, nostalgic feels:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

I just want to cry seeing the late stand-up comic introduce the former child star as his “TV daughter” as their arms are wrapped around each other. The emotions were already present when the Great American Media actress honored Saget through a series of photos. With each picture, it was clear that Saget didn't need to be Danny Tanner to show affection to his co-stars.

But seeing old clips of Saget with Bure reminded me why they made a great TV father/daughter duo on their show. Their familial chemistry on the ABC series was evident through every heartfelt talk, laugh and of course, hug.

As the former Hallmark Channel star was watching these clips, an emotional Bure revealed it was the first time she had ever seen them. While being “teary-eyed,” the Some Kind of Wonderful alum shared more about what she was thinking while reflecting on the good old days:

That was great! That was so fun to see. [...] Yeah, that was really emotional to see Bob. I just have so much love for him. I really do. He was such a good friend, such a loving person, and loved everyone so well. I miss him. I miss those hugs and the jokes.

The Full House alums truly appeared to have a friendship that stood the test of time. In fact, you could have called their friendship unlikely, as Bure couldn’t get into Saget's raunchy stand-up material. However, she said it was easy to be her TV dad’s friend, as she told herself to separate the comedian’s material from the "kindness" and "love" he brought out. Because the talented actress had known Saget since she was 11, it was no wonder they were still so close by the time the latter passed.

I’m glad that Candace Cameron Bure got to see her younger self with Bob Saget. As heartbreaking as it may be for me to watch those throwback clips, I’d like to believe it strengthens the love and memories she has with her old friend that’ll never go away. You can watch DJ and Danny navigate life together on Full House, which is streaming now with Disney+ subscription or an active Hulu subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3642. Square Enix Is Making Final Fantasy 14 Free For 30 Days For A Ton More People

If you are like me and haven’t played Final Fantasy XIV in a minute, now might be the time to jump back in and finally get through Dawntrail before the new expansion launches in 2027. Starting November 16, players who haven’t logged in to the paid MMORPG in the last five months (150 days specifically) are eligible for 30 days of free playtime.

Players have from November 16th to January 14, 2027 to claim their free 30 days, which means that, if you time it right, your free period will overlap with the launch of the $45 Evercold expansion on February 23. Square Enix has all the specifics here.

The Road to Evercold begins today, helping you prepare for the upcoming release of Evercold!

â­ 30-day Free Login Campaign â­ Tales of Adventure: Winter's Prelude

— FINAL FANTASY XIV (@en.finalfantasyxiv.com) 2026-11-16T10:30:05.686Z

Digging into the details, it seems like Square Enix knows a lot of people (including me) lit out after Endwalker and haven’t been back to play the latest expansion, Dawntrail. In addition to offering free game time, Square Enix is also offering a new $10 Tales of Adventure item which lets players auto-skip main story quest content. It’s designed specifically to leap-frog players over Dawntrail stuff, taking them from the end of Endwalker to the beginning of “In Fate’s Footsteps,” this year’s Evercold-introducing 7.5 event patch.

It is powerfully seductive to pay $10 bucks to take the coward’s way out of Dawntrail. I’ve heard that expansion is just okay, and possibly even worth skipping. But I play Final Fantasy XIV for its story. It can’t always be Heavensward or Shadowbringers, sometimes there has to be a Stormblood in there and that’s okay. As I try to take advantage of the free game time, I’ll finally see Dawntrail for myself.

#3641. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting much-requested split-screen multiplayer and new mode in 2027

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has announced.

Split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely new mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

"We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's currently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Company under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.

#3639. Booby-Trapped Video Game Console Explodes At Rival Gaming Store

A video game console exploded last month at a repair shop in Santo AndrÃ©, Brazil, injuring two of the people who worked there. Police are calling it an attempted murder, and say a rival business owner was trying to eliminate his competition. The man they think was responsible was arrested over the weekend as part of a separate investigation.

G1 Globo reports (via Dexerto) that the original incident took place on October 23 at around 5:30 p.m. A delivery person dropped off a gaming device for some sort of repair, but inside the retro gaming console, police say there was a concealed timer and two cylinders filled with flammable liquid. The store owner reportedly put the console inside a drawer where it later ignited, putting a hole in the ceiling as well as damaging other parts of the store.

EmpresÃ¡rio Ã© preso suspeito de enviar videogame com explosivos que detonaram em loja de eletrÃ´nicos de Santo AndrÃ©, Grande SP https://t.co/EqXSlkM1J9 #g1 pic.twitter.com/H3naAgNzlV

The store owner and someone else at the scene received minor injuries and burns. Civil Police have since charged local businessman Everton Yoshizumi Lima with attempted murder. They say he ran similar repair shops, including one on the same street where the victim had recently opened a new store, and was trying to eliminate competition.

The owner of the store that received the booby-trapped console said he had suffered previous attempts at sabotage as well. It’s not yet clear which console was used in the attack, though footage of the drop-off makes it look too small to be a PS5 or Xbox Series X.

The crew retention on Newell's boats is six times the average on other superyachts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leviathan, the 111-meter superyacht owned by Valve co-founder Gabe Newell, has a number of unconventional features. It has a pool for SCUBA testing. It has an NBA-regulation basketball court. An Aston-Martin can be found parked on its helipad. It forgoes the typical teakwood deck in favor of easier-to-clean synthetic flooring.

But for the industry experts at Superyacht Times, which recently released a walkthrough video of the Leviathan's features and operating philosophy (via GamesRadar), the most remarkable thing about Newell's roving wave-palace is its owner's willingness to appreciate the crew that enables his lifestyle of seaborne excess.

"The most surprising thing is what happens when we go through these doors," says Superyacht Times editor-in-chief Francesca Webster as she enters into an immaculate communal dining space on the Leviathan's main deck. "Rather than having the traditional saloon which we normally see on a superyacht—welcoming guests and being the first point of contact to the interior—Gabe actually opted to utilize this incredible space for the crew mess."

Instead of banishing his crew to whatever dank closets and canned rat-gruel might be typical for superyacht staff, Newell enjoys his meals alongside the crew each day. According to Superyacht Times, engaging in that sort of mutual humanity makes him a peculiarity among yachtfolk.

"It's all about shared experience on board his boats. And that is something that we've really never seen before in our industry," Webster says.

Having delivered a casual indictment of the pursuit of yachting in its entirety, we move on the Leviathan's owner deck, where we're shown one of a series of VIP cabins that would shame a top-of-the-line hotel. There, we see more of Newell's uncharacteristic acknowledgment that it would maybe be cool for the people who keep a luxury ship running to enjoy some of the luxury.

"One of the most unique things about Gabe, the ownership structure that he has and the way that he has a vision for yachting," Webster says, "is that this VIP cabin is also used by the crew."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

That vision was apparently a head-scratcher for the vessel's designers at Mark Bryman Design, who Webster says "found this to be quite an incredible challenge and an exciting opportunity to think about yachting from a different perspective and really turn the ownership experience on its head."

Given the video's faintly perplexed tone, Superyacht Times still appears somewhat puzzled by the idea. But the Leviathan's designers seem to have gotten a hold on things eventually: In addition to the crew mess and lavish cabins, the yacht also features a gaming center, outfitted with 15 PCs "for the crew, the guests, and Gabe himself to come and enjoy themselves."

The appreciation evidently goes both ways. Superyacht Times says superyachts retain a crewmember for six to nine months, on average. Newell's crews, however, tend to stay on for an average of four and a half years—a figure that would undoubtedly be lower if he never got over his Mongolian throat singing phase.

#3637. A Ton Of Big Blockbuster Games Are Already On Sale For Black Friday 2026

Black Friday seems to arrive earlier and earlier each year. It’s gone from a single-day event into a month-long deals bonanza where a ton of the discounts are fake. For gaming, the Black Friday “season” is already well underway, and actually a bunch of the deals are pretty good.

Marvel’s Wolverine was a surprising miss for Sony’s first-party PlayStation game factory, but it delivers on spectacle and cinematic comic-book storylines, and it’s currently just $50, which is a very good price for a big-budget blockbuster that came out less than three months ago.

There are a bunch of other recent games that are pretty cheap, too, as well as some older ones:

The other big highlight on this list is 007 First Light, an action-adventure from the makers of Hitman that will probably appear on a bunch of people’s best games of 2026 lists. It’s half off digitally on PS5 right now. Star Wars Zero Company, another strong release this year, is also on sale. Saros, a fairly challenging 3D bullet hell shooter, is more of an acquired taste, but also easy to recommend at just $40.

Final shout-outs go to Borderlands 4 and Mafia: The Old Country. Published by the same company, they couldn’t be more different. Borderlands is a grindy RPG loot shooter with a silly sense of humor. Mafia is a narrative-driven cinematic adventure that you can finish in just 10-12 hours. It’s perfect for people who want a rock-solid game that’s not caught up in all of the minutia and busywork of most modern gaming blockbusters.

At $20 a piece, they’re both a steal. Why so many steep discounts so early in November? Probably to catch your attention before Grand Theft Auto 6 drops in just a few days.

Spoilers for Season 2, Episode 6 of Marshals are ahead! You can stream the series with a Paramount+ subscription and catch new episodes on CBS every Sunday.

The episode of Marshals that just aired on the 2026 TV schedule is inspired by a tragedy that actually happened to one of its stars and American Indian Affairs Coordinator, Mo Brings Plenty, and his family. In 2024, his nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, died, and a coroner ruled out foul play. His family disagreed with that, and they’re still looking for answers. In this week's episode of Marshals, Mo’s nephew, Troy, is found dead, and he and Kayce work to prove that it was a murder, not suicide. Ultimately, the case is left unsolved, and according to Mo Brings Plenty, that was a very important detail to include.

Knowing that “Roughstock” was inspired by his own experiences, I asked Mo Brings Plenty, who plays Mo in Marshals and Yellowstone, about details in the episode he was happy to see included. He immediately noted that he was glad the case was left unsolved, because that kind of outcome happens in real life, often, as the actor explained:

Oh, I was happy to see that when the police officer said he just kind of blew it off, because that's really the case. And so I was happy that we showed that legitimate part of it. Not every officer is that way, but in some cases, in some states - primarily states that have a high American Indian population - that occurs.

When I spoke to Mo in March this year about an episode of Marshals having to do with missing American Indians, he told me they “haven’t got any answers for” what happened to his nephew, Cole.

In this episode of Marshals, it’s made very clear that while Troy’s case will stay open, it will likely go unsolved. It’s obvious that it’s not being prioritized by law enforcement, and despite the marshals best efforts, there is no solution as to who killed Troy by the end of the episode. When I asked Mo why it was important for this episode to go without a solution to Troy’s case, he said:

Because the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us as American Indian people, and of course we're tax-paying people as well. And so, you know, first responders get their funding through taxpayers, tax funding, and so when it doesn't work for us, then it's so frustrating. It's like, ‘Well, why are we even paying taxes?’ And so that's one of the things that is impactful for me, and that I need to continue to speak about because it is occurring.

In the case of Mo’s real nephew, Cole, he was found dead a few days after he was reported missing and named as a suspect in a domestic violence case. Two years later, Mo spoke to THR and claimed that his nephew’s death had gone “uninvestigated,” while the Lawrence Police Department said there was “no foul play involved in Cole’s death.”

When I spoke to Mo about this topic recently and how it was represented on this Yellowstone show, he said:

It's sad for me and my family, especially when I hear the cry for other nationalities and in foreign countries, when the very same thing is occurring to us as the original inhabitants within this country, we're basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields.

According to the U.S. Department of the Interior Indian Affairs, there are “approximately 4,200 missing and murder cases that have gone unsolved.” And when I asked Mo Brings Plenty if Marshals could ever circle back to Troy’s unsolved case, he said:

Absolutely, it could definitely happen. But you know, there are so many stories. I mean, my family is not the only family. This isn't the first time something like this has occurred in real life. You know, there are many stories, many families, different situations, different circumstances that are going through the same thing.

Overall, he was clear that there are lots of stories like his that should be shown on Kayce’s Yellowstone spinoff. He’s not the only one who has lost a loved one in this way and was left without answers, and he’s hoping to see more of those stories depicted on Marshals.

Now, to see how Mo’s story continues, you can watch the next episode of Marshals on November 22 at 8:30 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Paramount+.

#3635. Beto O’Rourke Says He’d “Do Anything” for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa—Including Work for Them

After the shocking Democratic victories in Texas last week, it was hard not to look over the shoulders of James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa and see the shadow of Beto O’Rourke, whose losses for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022 had become cautionary tales of Democratic hopelessness in Texas. And perhaps proof that nice guys couldn’t win. But in the years after those failed runs, O’Rourke never really went away. He launched a voter-registration group called Powered by People, punched out missives on Substack, livestreamed his thoughts, and quietly advised his party from the background.

“Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019?” O’Rourke says now, looking back at the cover story I wrote, in which he proclaimed he was “just born to be in it,” a premature declaration that almost immediately sank his prospects. “I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.”

O'Rourke taks the stage during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally at the Texas Capitol in August 2025.

Like Stacey Abrams in Georgia, who lost her own race for governor but used her visibility to build a stronger coalition, O’Rourke can claim some credit for setting the table for Democratic success in Texas. Talarico won his first race, for a Republican-held state House seat, on O’Rourke’s 2018 wave. And as it turns out, O’Rourke himself weighed another Senate run this year. When Talarico asked whether he’d run, O’Rourke said only if Talarico ran for governor instead, eventually stepping aside after concluding that the moment called for “something and someone new.” When he launched his Senate campaign, Talarico said he wanted to replicate O’Rourke’s “energy.”

O’Rourke, meanwhile, became a behind-the-scenes player: Powered by People was one of four partners in the Texas Democrats’ $30 million coordinated campaign, and it says it reached more than 110,000 new and young voters in Texas this cycle. Ken Paxton noticed and tried to put O’Rourke “behind bars” for funding the Democrats who fled the state to block its Donald Trump–backed redistricting.

O’Rourke says the wave cascaded so far down the ballot in Texas that a candidate who tried backing out of her campaign before Election Day ended up winning. “At that point it was too late to take her name off the ballot,” he says. “She didn’t campaign, just won her election. That speaks to the magnitude of the wave, but also to the value of having a fighter on every front. Somebody said to me, ‘A wave’s great, even better if you have a surfboard.’”

Over an hour-long conversation, O’Rourke parses the political revolution in his home state, suggests how Democrats can hold on to their land grab, and, perhaps unsurprisingly, looks ahead to another run for office.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: The conventional wisdom is that this was a revolt against Trump, and that the candidates and the Democratic strategy were secondary. What’s your read?

Beto O’Rourke: So much of this election was a rejection of Trump and Trumpism: the corruption, the wars, the cruelty. But after 2024, people were anxious that we didn’t have a unifying national leader. [Joe] Biden was not going to be it. Kamala Harris turned out not to be it. President Obama, I think wisely, held back…. Chuck Schumer was persona non grata in any gathering of Democrats. The DNC was in the red.

What it did was allow for candidates in different parts of the country to really establish themselves in their own right and by their own merits, never having to fear being under the shadow of a larger figure. It’s really a blessing. That’s how you get Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, Mary Peltola, all these extraordinary candidates who are extraordinarily different from each other. In Texas, for the first time in half a century, Democrats fielded a fighter on every front: 150 state House candidates, 38 congressional candidates, 16 state Senate candidates. You had to have a historically terrible, corrupt president. But you also had to have this historically beaten-down Democratic Party; that the Democrats don’t have a message, they don’t have a leader. That all turned out to be a great thing.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

A year ago you convened Talarico, Colin Allred, and Joaquin Castro to think about a statewide slate. Talarico went his own way. You warned him he’d “want friends on that ticket.” What did you mean?

I just wanted to win, and I put that before anything else. James and I had many conversations before he officially announced. He asked me, “Are you interested? Would you run?” And I told him, “The only condition on which I would run is if you were to run for governor, or somebody else who could draw that kind of attention and resources, and if we had the ticket rounded out by strong contenders for every position on the ballot.”

My advice to him was: “Look, I’ve done this before. No matter how talented you are, no matter how much you can raise, this state is so big, the Republicans are so entrenched, you need a fighter on every front.” And ultimately, that’s what happened. Gina really hit her stride at the right time. Her strength as a candidate a year ago compared to how she finished is worlds apart, and that is a testament to what an exceptional leader she is.

Clearly, it was the right call for James to be there. He is just an extraordinarily talented communicator. He was a phenomenally focused candidate. He was absolutely the right guy for the moment. I also think it was the right call for Jasmine Crockett to run too. I know from being on college campuses how electrifying she is, how many young people she brought into the electorate this time. They stayed in even after Jasmine was defeated in the primary.

The Atlantic reported that you told Hinojosa, “Not one person can win Texas. It has to be two.” Is that what you said?

I definitely spoke to Gina before she made the decision to run, and then after. To be honest with you, I can’t remember if I said “two.” What I said consistently to everybody who was thinking about it—Colin, Joaquin, Gina, Jasmine [Crockett], James—was that you need a fighter on every front and the strongest possible ticket. That was based on the last run I had, in 2022, and even the ’18 run. If Joaquin or Julián Castro had run for governor when I was running for Senate, who knows? Of course, at that time, we didn’t know the size of the wave that was about to crash.

I definitely did. I could have run…. You’d have to ask James, but I think he probably would have supported that if I had. We have an amazing organization in waiting, volunteers who’ve been with me, the ability to raise money. But was that the right thing to do? No. I had been before Texas twice before, and the moment demanded something different and, I would argue, something better.

You can’t discount a politician’s ambition and ego. I had to find a way to get past that. It helped having conversations with my wife. It helped having conversations with our kids. It helped having conversations with people who’d been on these runs with me before. Also, I spent a lot of time traveling Texas. My love language is a town hall meeting, where it’s just a free-for-all and anybody can step to the mic and ask any questions. At the end of that, I really felt this moment called for something and someone new. I don’t know that Texas could have produced a stronger—I was going to say candidate, but really a one-two punch. It was James and Gina. They’re both exceptional individually. Together, they transcended what had happened in politics for as long as I’ve been alive.

Honestly, my own doubt about whether Texas could be won was based on you. We’d seen this story before.

I wouldn’t have done this work as a volunteer for the last four years if I didn’t believe in Texas. I know in my heart and in my bones that we are so much better than the people in power. It’s the obscene abortion ban that has cost the lives of girls and women, the $7.25-an-hour minimum wage, the fact that we’re the least insured state in the country. Four years after Uvalde, and no one in power has done a single thing. It’s insane having Texas Republicans say, if you’re Muslim, regardless of whether you’re an immigrant, you should be deported from this country. That’s just not who we are.

O'Rourke speaks during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally, where 5,000 people attended. Attendees protested proposed redistricting, immigration enforcement, and other Trump-backed legislation and proposed changes.

When I ran for governor, 9 million registered voters didn’t cast a ballot. It’s not because they don’t care; it’s not that they’re lazy. This state makes it harder than any other to participate, so we’ve got to try that much harder. I knew it was a matter of time and effort. The greater the effort, the shorter the time. But did I know it would be 2026? Did I know it would be every statewide office and the state House? Fuck no, man. Nobody knew that.

Ken Paxton called you a “repeat loser” and tried to prosecute your PAC. He lost by 12 points.

We’ve spent more than $600,000; we have Powered by People defending our organization, defending me. He accused me of bribery. He tried to remove the license for Powered by People to do voter-registration work in the state of Texas. He promised to lock me up, to put me behind bars. The 15th Court of Appeals [judges], all of whom were appointed by Greg Abbott, so none of them friends of mine, have ruled against Paxton for attacking somebody for exercising their First Amendment rights. Do I think that I’m going to get that money back? I don’t know.

Couldn’t have happened to a better person.

Did Talarico and Hinojosa acknowledge your role, or did they keep their distance?

You’d have to ask them. I got a really nice message from James on election night, and I had a chance to campaign with Gina in the closing days of the election. That’s not an easy choice for Gina, right? Both of them did an exceptional job of being themselves and not seeming to be beholden to anybody. They invited nobody in from outside of Texas, and we all understood: This is their show. So getting to campaign with Gina here at the University of Texas at El Paso, at the University of Houston, it was really nice to hear her acknowledge the work that so many of us have been doing, especially all these volunteers who’ve been out there, whose names most people will never know.

I’ve known them both for a decade. James and I were on the campaign trail together in 2017 and 2018, when he was running his first race for state House in Williamson County. Somebody just sent me a picture of the two of us at an event in Williamson in 2017. These are really fucking good human beings, and they’re also really good at understanding power and how to win it. It is so rare that those two things come together.

O'Rourke speaks during a "Fighting Oligarchy" event in Houston, Texas on Oct. 20, 2026.

Are Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries the right leaders for this moment?

Chuck Schumer absolutely is not. Early 2025, [Elon] Musk is running wild with DOGE, Trump is steamrolling every center of power. They’re all bending the knee—the Ivy Leagues, the big law firms, the media companies. Hakeem marshaled every Democratic vote in the House but one to stop Trump, DOGE, and Musk, and the deal with Schumer was going to do the same. Then, inexplicably, Schumer bent the knee as well. In that moment, it was absolutely over for me.

Schumer deserves so much credit and praise for his work over the decades. But he doesn’t deserve to be majority leader at this major turning point for the country, not when you have James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, or Jon Ossoff. We have an embarrassment of talent in the Senate right now, and we should use it. The age when any American cares what the majority leader reads on the Senate floor is over. I don’t even know what his message is, and that says something.

Hakeem Jeffries hasn’t had the chance to lead as Speaker. We were elected in the same class in 2012, and I’m grateful that he stood strong early in the Trump administration. I wish he could communicate more effectively than he has so far. Maybe there’s a scenario where he’s Speaker, but he taps the far better communicators in his caucus, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to do more of that work, and he’s focused on getting the legislative results.

Eleven House Democrats missed the vote to impeach [Pete] Hegseth, enough to have changed the outcome. What happened there?

Eleven is a big number. That certainly invites some conspiracy thinking, or, maybe just as bad, the idea that these folks aren’t up to the job. It’s really important that the Democratic leadership in the House address this directly, explain what happened, and take ownership and responsibility for it.

You’ve said Democrats wasted their power in 2009 and 2021, and that next time they should “drive that car like we stole it.” What happens in the first 100 days?

Right off the bat, you have to make our lives better in a way that we can feel. In Texas, that’s not hard, because we are in such a fucking hole. Raise the minimum wage from $7.25. Expand Medicaid when the federal government’s paying 90 cents on the dollar. Stop this voucher thing that is draining tax dollars from local schools, and pay teachers so they don’t have to work a second or third job.

Nationally, you have to do the same. The response to this from many is that Trump has the power of the pen and will veto that. Make him veto that. I don’t like anything about him, but I don’t know that there’s a more successful political operator than Trump. I don’t think there’s someone who reads power better than he does. Maybe there are deals to be had. Maybe you force the veto, and you set up a clear contrast going into 2028. At a minimum, you have to get caught trying.

The huge issues that Democrats have absolutely failed to lead on, we have to lead on now, so that would include immigration and that would include democracy. Immigration was arguably the issue that voters made their decisions on in 2016 and 2024, and if we continue to hope that it’s just going to solve itself, instead of making tough choices and using political capital on this, then it’s going to be our demise in future elections as well. [On democracy], there’s no democracy to restore or save. There is a democracy you can build anew. Getting corporations out of politics; what just passed in Montana is potentially a wonderful precedent from which we could build. Getting a voting rights act passed again. [Pushing] the popular-vote compact; I think we have enough trifectas now. I’m probably in the minority in the Democratic Party, but I’m a big believer in term limits. People give a speech and are like, “We’ve got to overturn Citizens United,” or, “We’ve got to do away with the Electoral College.” That’s a great applause line, but when is that ever going to happen?

O'Rourke spoke in October 2026 as the fight for the Senate came down to the wire.

The big dig on Democrats is: You talked a great game on immigration, then you won the White House; you had the House and the Senate. You didn’t do anything. You talked a great game about voting rights. You had the trifecta, and you didn’t do anything. Now we have the power. We’d better deliver, or watch out.

I’m surprised I’m not hearing more from you about prosecutions and subpoenas. You spent the last two years warning about fascism and calling for accountability.

That’s got to be part of it too. The law is king in this country; no one’s above it, no one’s below it. We’ve allowed the precedent, through the Epstein crimes, that you can be rich enough and well-connected enough to rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity. I spent a lot of time with young people doing this voter-registration work, and that is probably the number one thing I hear from them for why they don’t vote: This shit doesn’t work. Ghislaine Maxwell [went to jail], but no man who actually did this has gone to prison or even faced trial.

Then there’s the corruption that flows from the president through his family, through his Cabinet officials, through the oligarchs [with whom] he surrounds himself. If we let this stand, much the way that we let stand his crimes against this country on January 6, 2021, that sets the most dangerous precedent. Look at the Roman Republic. It wasn’t Caesar crossing the Rubicon. It was Sulla turning his armies against Rome, and there was never a consequence or accountability for that, so the precedent was set and Caesar picked that up. [Editor’s note: O’Rourke is an avid fan of the podcast The Rest Is History.] There will be a more capable, powerful demagogue than Trump—he or she may be a Democrat; he or she may be a Republican—who will use that precedent unless that door is closed. I know this is an unpopular thing to talk about within our party, because folks want to turn the page. But that keeps biting us in the ass. Everyone who went to prison for [January 6] was pardoned by this president.

But if you spend the next two years investigating him and prices stay high, Democrats are cooked.

That’s exactly right. That’s why I said you’ve got to deliver for people, and they have to feel it immediately. Democrats are responsible for so many good things that are both slow-working and expressed through the tax code, like the child tax credit, and for which they don’t claim credit. Those things have to change.

I was in the Rio Grande Valley after 2020, doing voter registration, knocking on doors, and talking to this guy who voted for Trump. I said, “You had a front-row seat to kids in cages, to family separation, to this cruelty here. Tell me what’s going on.” And he said, “I hate all that stuff, but voting on those issues when I can’t feed my family and I may lose my home is a luxury. I don’t have that luxury.” We have to learn that lesson. You’ve got to make people’s lives better, and if you do that, you build trust and legitimacy: “Okay, these guys are really helping me. They really reflect my values and my interests. And now that they are pursuing these investigations and this accountability, I trust them, and I know that, regardless of the outcome of these investigations, my life is better because they are in power.”

If Trump felt that he or his family were under real legal threat, is there any world in which investigations become a chip to trade, say, for immigration reform? I realize this is very Trumpy thinking, but you are dealing with Trump.

No. Totally understandable, and it’s a recognition of how politics and power typically work. But part of how we got Trump in the first place was that there weren’t consequences for massive failures or crimes committed: these banks that were bailed out after they had driven so many Americans into poverty and homelessness in 2008 and 2009, these wars the Bush administration launched on false pretenses. They lied to us, they lied to the world, and it took the lives of so many Americans, Iraqis, and Afghans. Never any consequence or accountability.

This corruption has been so flagrant, it’s as though Trump and those closest to him were daring America to hold them accountable. Then there’s the open defiance of the law and the Constitution: killing people on fishing boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping a head of state, launching a war and continuing it in violation of the War Powers Act. When you allow these things to stand, they become the precedent. But if there’s accountability, then that becomes the precedent upon which future leaders will be able to act. Trump may feel he’s fighting for his life, that he’s backed into a corner. He may make it harder for Democrats to do the things that they need to do. But I don’t think we can operate in fear of him.

Some Democrats, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, argue that the corruption and the high prices are the same story. Do you buy that?

Talarico is masterful at saying that: Their corruption is costing you and your family. So many examples in Texas. Billionaires bought off Governor Greg Abbott and persuaded him to pursue a voucher scheme that took public dollars out of local schools and sent them to private schools, decreased the quality of your school, and raised your local property taxes to make up the difference. Abbott, beholden to corporate interests, opened the door [to data centers], and our electricity prices went up and the quality of our water and air was compromised.

O'Rourke says he doesn't know if there’s an office he can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030.

The biggest one was in 2021, when we had the winter storm. In the energy capital of the world, they couldn’t keep the lights on or the power running, and pipeline operators [and others in the energy industry], among the biggest donors to Greg Abbott, began to price-gouge, bankrupting utilities and causing ratepayers to pay sky-high prices. One of the pipeline operator CEOs wrote Abbott a $1 million check at the end of that winter storm, almost as if to say thank you for not prosecuting them. It’s not corruption in an abstract way; it’s corruption that’s costing you. And yes, that corruption should be prosecuted. It’s not enough to just win the election and throw the bums out. If the bums broke the law, then they have to face the consequences.

If Democrats hold this ground, it would seem to open the door for you again. Is there an office you can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030?

I don’t know, and people would have to answer that question for me. That’s what I’ve been trying to do these last four years, just listen to people and figure out where I can be most useful. I’ve tried to remain agnostic.

I had a conversation earlier in the year with somebody who just won in Texas, and they had been one of the people to encourage me to run for governor in 2022—what the fuck was I thinking, running in Joe Biden’s midterm?—and I asked them, “Did you think I had any chance to win?” And they said, “Oh God, no.” But they knew that we needed somebody to galvanize the state, protect our gains in Harris County, and shore up the wins that we’d [earned] in 2018. Somebody had to carry us through that next stage of the relay.

Just so I’m clear, I would not have run if I didn’t think there was a chance we could win in 2022. It was an incredibly tough environment that got tougher and tougher as the race proceeded. But it did a lot of good, and in some small way it was probably helpful toward what happened in 2026.

When [my wife] Amy and I made the decision in 2016 that we had to do something, I went to everyone: Joaquin and Julián Castro, Clay Jenkins, Michael Sorrell, Wendy Davis. I asked each of them, “Will you run? If you do, I will get behind you.” Ultimately, I was like, “Okay, if you guys aren’t going to do it, I am going to do it. I know this is crazy, and I know all of you are better positioned, I’m going to do it.” So if I feel the way that I felt that time, that I’m the right person for this, then, whatever the odds, I’m going to get out there. But if running could hurt us, if there’s somebody better—and that was a conclusion I drew coming into this cycle—then please step up, and I’ll get out of the way and support you as a volunteer.

The next statewide race in Texas is 2030. One thing I’m thinking about right now is 2028, and the fact that the 40 Electoral College votes in Texas are ours to lose. I want to be part of the team getting Texas ready for that nominee to win our state. I’m happy to follow James and Gina’s lead. They’re our leaders now.

Can you imagine working in a Hinojosa administration?

I will do anything for her, and the same for James. It’s just crazy, hearing that.

What about taking Powered by People to Florida? They could use some help, evidently.

These states of the former Confederacy have worked so hard to make it hard for people, especially young people, to vote. We don’t have Election Day data yet, but through early voting, 60% of our voters, overwhelmingly 18 to 29 years old, voted through early voting. That’s about 33 points ahead of the average for that demographic in Texas. I sure wish our party had put resources behind [Angie] Nixon and [David] Jolly in Florida. We could have won those races. What was [the margin] in the governor’s race? 1.3%. Heartbreaking. If I can be useful there, I’m happy to go.

About a year after my 2019 story came out, I texted you that I hoped there were no hard feelings, and you took responsibility for your own errors. It seems like you’ve been through a process since then.

That’s just life, right? I truly feel so incredibly lucky: getting to serve in Congress, getting to run for the US Senate, being considered for the nomination in 2020, being back out on the trail for governor, and then doing this work with Powered by People. When I get depressed is when I don’t have purpose. Then I’m prone to feel sorry for myself or to wonder what if. I’m a big believer that action is the antidote to despair. So I try not to dwell too much on decisions that I’ve made. Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019? I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look at where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.

Joe Rogan suggested on his podcast that Talarico should run for president. Any advice for him?

I am the last guy to give Talarico advice, because he’s just been so freaking smart and amazing. Whether he runs for president, whether he serves out his full term in the Senate, he is one of very few leaders in this country who have met the moment. I trust him to make the best decisions for, first and foremost, the country, for Texas, and then for himself.

Who excites you in the 2028 field? You’ve got Gavin Newsom on the center-left, and AOC and Ro Khanna presenting themselves as heirs to Bernie Sanders.

We could have added another 15 people to that list. There was a lot of gnashing of teeth two years ago: We don’t have a national leader; what is Democrats’ message? That was liberating for all of these candidates, and you’re going to have so many diverse perspectives in 2028. What you did these last 10 years is going to be an important consideration. Gavin Newsom was one of the first national Democrats to recognize what Trump was trying to do by redrawing these congressional maps, starting in Texas, and I was really impressed with how quickly he moved and how strong he was on offense. Pete Buttigieg has been nonstop traveling the country supporting candidates. In the wake of 2024, with this sense of total defeat, a few people just got out there, and AOC was one of them. I like the folks who never stop fighting, who are true to themselves and not susceptible to the prevailing winds. Bernie Sanders is probably the best example of that.

Ro Khanna and I, when we were in Congress together, authored the No PAC Act. We asked our legislative staffs, “Can you find out who last authored a bill like this so we can amend it and improve it and make it our own?” There was no bill. Nobody had ever done that. He’s been so consistently focused on democracy. Greg Casar, he’s from Texas. He’s the chair of the [Congressional] Progressive Caucus and also has been crisscrossing the country. There are a lot of good people out there.

O'Rourke speaks at a campaign rally at the University of Houston on October 20, 2026.

After 2016 and 2024, a lot of women I know concluded that this country won’t elect a woman president. Can a woman be elected?

Absolutely. Gina Hinojosa—here in Texas, the conventional wisdom was that if a Democrat ever wins, it’s got to be a straight white man who fits the following characteristics. And here you have the first Latina from the border. It’s fucking awesome. It’s going to sound corny, but I really believe in this country, and that faith was vindicated last Tuesday. It wasn’t the country being like, “Go Democrats!” It was the country saying, “We can do better, and we’re going to take a chance on folks who may not fit the profile.” I think that holds true for the country in 2028.

You just turned 54. If you never ran again, would you be okay with that?

I think about it sometimes. Is the prize the office—junior senator from the state of Texas, president of the United States of America? Or is the prize a much better world for my kids and this country? I always want that to be the answer, and it is. I just fucking won the lottery in life. Our kids are absolutely thriving; my oldest is about to be 20, middle kid is 18, my youngest just turned 16. I’ve been lucky with Amy and living in El Paso, getting to do this fulfilling work.

But just to be clear: Would I love to serve in office again at some point? Absolutely. The El Paso City Council may have been my most fulfilling time in politics. Loved being in Congress—what a high honor. But if it doesn’t happen, I’m more than okay. I’m the luckiest guy out there. I’m good, no matter what happens.

Let's talk about what we know about the situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Warning! The following contains spoilers from the 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way episode "Out Of The Frying Pan, Into The Family." Stream the episode with an HBO Max subscription, and read at your own risk!

Niles Valentine has kept his wife, Matilda, in the dark since the start of the 2026 TV schedule about his plan to move to Ghana. He finally decided to drop the bombshell in this latest episode, and predictably, she was pretty upset to learn he was no longer working toward bringing her to the United States. Given her anger, there was a possibility this married 90 Day couple could split at the end of the season.

With various rumors floating around the internet about their status, I decided to do a bit of digging to see what I could find on whether series veterans Niles and Matilda are still together. While I didn't expect either of them to break their contract agreements and explicitly say one way or another, I think it's safe to say it looks like they're still together, with some predictable updates.

Niles posted a photo on Instagram of what appeared to be the inside of an apartment in the United States back on November 13th. Readers can take a look at the post below, in which he showed the difference someone's posture can make. Take a look:

A post shared by Niles Valentine (@roman_cupid_95)

That doesn't look like any room in Matilda's apartment, which has me guessing he's back in the United States at this point. I can't claim to be an expert on apartments in Africa, but I've lived in a good deal of American ones that have that exact same look when it comes to the bathroom!

Niles returning home feels like the most obvious outcome in this season of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way. Matilda married him in the hopes of coming to the United States and not just having a better life for herself but for her family back in Africa as well. She's obviously mad that Niles couldn't make it happen as soon as he promised, but that doesn't mean she wants him to give up.

If Niles has returned to the US, I think it's fair to speculate that he and Matilda are still together. The pair still follow each other on Instagram, which usually feels like an obvious sign that 90 Day couples are still together and married.

Why 90 Day Fiancé's New Florida Spinoff Has Me Questioning If We've Lost The Plot

If we get to the end of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way and learn that Niles is still working to bring Matilda to the United States, I won't be surprised. That's been the goal from the start, and I think he made a rash decision to move to Africa without looking into how difficult it would be for him to start a life in the country.

Niles may not be incredibly wealthy, but his earning potential in the United States is likely higher than it would be in Ghana. Even if she doesn't have her husband with her, I can understand wanting to wait as long as it takes for him to find a way to bring her to the United States rather than changing the plan.

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way continues on TLC on Sundays at 8:00 p.m. ET. We'll see how things shake out for Niles and Matilda down the stretch, and keep an eye on the other couples taking part as well.

#3632. Democrats Plot (and Party) in Washington After Midterms Rout

This is the November 12, 2026 edition of Party Animals, a letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Good evening from Washington, where Party Animals is coming to grips with how the social scene in the capital will change amidst a dramatic transfer of power. Gone will be the heady days of President Donald Trump’s total control of the US government. The next two years will be defined by how his administration handles a muscular Democratic opposition.

At Crooked Con, a conference put on the weekend after the midterm elections by the media company founded by former Obama staffers and Pod Save America hosts Jon Favreau, Tommy Vietor, and Jon Lovett, I got a sense of just how confident the party is after almost two years in the wilderness.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Befitting the sensibilities of the incoming Congress, Crooked week kicked off with a surprise appearance from Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who wore keffiyeh-patterned Air Force 1s to the live taping of his Pod Save America episode. The crowd went ballistic.

In this edition of Party Animals, the view from Washington’s new libbed-up social scene; what a Newsmax show says about Trump’s tumbling popularity among young Americans; and my colleague Joe Hagan’s interview with Beto O’Rourke, the original Democrat-who-might-win-Texas, about how the party finally pulled it off in the Lone Star State.

Also mentioned in this issue: Barrett Adair, Matthew Foldi, Robert Garcia, Katie Miller, Felicia Schwartz, Keith Edwards, Vaughn Hillyard, Marc Beckman, Marco Rubio, Michael Scherer, Chi Ossé, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be aired on Newsmax. Praise will be debated and affirmed by a Crooked Con panel.

I doubt there were many places on earth more buoyant than Crooked Con in DC last weekend. The conference brought together a legion of newly elected Democrats, veteran members of Congress, journalists, and liberal content creators for a day of live plotting that culminated in a party at City Tap House, where Robert Garcia, the incoming emperor of Oversight, worked the room. “I was pretty optimistic going into the election, but this is beyond anything I imagined,” Favreau tells Party Animals. “The majority of the country is clearly ready to move on from the Trump show and give Democrats another chance.”

The creators were ecstatic. At an after-after-party nearby, Barrett Adair, a platinum blonde progressive with more than 200,000 TikTok followers, bounced around in a hot-pink latex dress. Pints were passed about so generously that once I had acquired three, I stopped bothering to tell which was which. Keith Edwards and Chi Ossé chatted intently in the corner. The night felt like a portent of what was to come: After nearly two years of the MAGA Huns marauding freely throughout the capital, the libs were soon to be back in charge—of Congress, at least. They celebrated accordingly.

“There's a lot to feel good about,” said Favreau. “Now we have to make it count.”

As the country grapples with the sheer magnitude of the blue wave that crashed down last week, our nation’s besuited analysts are seeking to identify the warning signs, like a postdisaster reconnaissance team examining the swell of a tsunami after it has decimated a Southeast Asian beach town. How did Trump lose the key voting blocs, like young men, that vaulted him back to power in 2024?

I’d like to propose a bellwether: The Big Beautiful Trump Show, an unsubtle program that debuted on conservative network Newsmax in October. It’s unclear whose brilliant idea it was to launch a North Korea–style propaganda show in support of a historically unpopular president weeks before he led his party into a generational election wipeout, but the show was hosted for three episodes by a DC-based influencer named Matthew Foldi. A source shared the ratings: The show debuted to 1,000 viewers in the younger demographic, the 25–54 age group coveted by advertisers. “Insanely low,” the source explained. A Newsmax spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Pour one out (a pint of raw milk, perhaps) for Katie Miller’s podcast, which is going on hiatus. I was a loyal listener—she booked pretty much every Trump Cabinet member, even the shy ones, and the friendly setting elicited more insight than you’d typically get out of a guarded pol like Marco Rubio. In a post on X, Miller said she would be pausing the show due to her husband’s new role as Trump’s chief of staff, writing that “the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.” The next day, The Atlantic’s Michael Scherer reported that Miller had signed a contract with Paramount for a future podcast deal, but that she had ended that as well. Paramount spokesperson Melissa Zukerman told Party Animals, “I don’t see she has anything with us.” When asked if Miller ever had a contract with Paramount, Zukerman did not respond.

Huang Out: The Economist does the important math and estimates that Jensen Huang’s Chinese affair “could go down as the most expensive shag in history.”

The Mayflower Millers: Read Kevin D. Williamson, of The Dispatch, on Stephen Miller and the incomprehensible case of the “heritage American.”

Dems in Vogue: Model Caroline Trentini reflects on her photo shoot with Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand, shot by Steven Meisel for a 2004 issue of Vogue Italia. I’m reliably told that these photos went quadruple platinum on Tumblr.

Cyberyuck: Read my colleague Nate Freeman’s soaring eulogy for the Cybertruck, Elon Musk’s grand experiment in bad taste.

Remember that 007 First Light song Lana Del Rey surprised-dropped earlier this year that I said wasn't very good because, as I put it at the time, "it sounds like Bond karaoke"? Well anyway, it's up for a Grammy Award.

007 First light, composed by Joe Henson and Alexis Leon Smith, is in the running in the "Best Score Soundtrack For Videogames and Other Interactive Media" category, alongside four other contenders:

I haven't heard any of the other tracks in contention (in my defense, neither Ghost of Yotei nor Wolverine are available on PC, and I actively dislike Star Wars) but after listening to the 007 First Light theme again, and with more time to think about it, I will say this: My initial assessment was absolutely correct.

This is not a good Bond theme. Lana Del Rey may be tremendously talented, but that's lost in the all-consuming effort to hit all the notes without understanding what connects them: The end result is a pale imitation built out of a musical stereotype that's readily identifiable as someone trying really hard to do a Bond theme based on what they were told a Bond theme is supposed to sound like.

The Grammy Awards are a music industry award, not a game award, and that means some games that you might expect to be nominated are sometimes excluded: The rules for the videogame category state that "videogames that contain music but are not available as stand-alone audio streams/releases" are not eligible for consideration, for example. So if you don't see your favorite of the year in the list, that might be why.

The videogame soundtrack category is relatively new: The Grammy Awards only added it in 2022. Previous winners include:

Anyway, will being a bad Bond theme keep 007 First Light from winning a major music industry award? The 2027 Grammy Awards take place on February 7, 2027—we'll find out then.
